extracted.intended_audience: researchers, students, and practitioners studying or creating humor (comedians, comedy writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the benign-violation theory to assess whether a joke produces humor by being simultaneously a violation and benign; includes identifying types of violations and mechanisms (norm detachment, psychological distance, reinterpretation) that render a violation harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition: simultaneous violation and benign perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor emerges when three simultaneous conditions are met: 1) A situation is a violation; 2) The situation is benign; 3) Both perceptions occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central criterion: a candidate joke must simultaneously (a) contradict expectations or standards and (b) be perceived as harmless/acceptable; both must be held at once for humor to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation occurs when circumstances contradict someone's expectations about how reality should function — something that 'threatens the way that you believe the world "ought" to be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include physical threats (tickling, play fighting), psychological threats (insults, sarcasm), and norm violations across social, cultural, linguistic, logical, and moral domains. When evaluating, identify which expectation or norm is being breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation must be perceived as benign — harmless, acceptable, or otherwise non-threatening — even though it is a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benignness can arise via weak commitment to the violated norm, availability of alternative norms/interpretations, psychological distance, or reinterpretation. Assess whether observers can plausibly construe the violation as harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity of perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both perceptions — that a situation is a violation and that it is benign — must be held at the same time by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience only sees the violation (too threatening) or only the benign aspect (too safe/boring), the humor will likely fail. Check whether both cognitive/emotional stances co-occur in the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm detachment / alternative norms
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation appears harmless when observers lack genuine commitment to the violated standard or when an alternative interpretation/norm makes the behavior acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: non-religious observers finding humor in religious-rule breaches, puns that shift interpretive norms. Evaluate audience commitment to the norm and whether alternative norms are available to render the violation benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The violation feels safer because of separation in time, space, social relation, or reality (e.g., it happened long ago, to someone else, or in fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of distance: temporal (past events), spatial (far away), social (affecting outsiders), and ontological (fictional scenarios). The heuristic 'comedy is tragedy plus time' captures this mechanism. Assess whether the audience has sufficient distance to perceive benignness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative framework reframes the violation so that its threatening meaning is reduced or inverted (e.g., playfighting framed as play).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contextual cues or frames (e.g., play signals, ironic tone) that let observers reinterpret the violation as non-threatening. Reinterpretation often depends on shared framing conventions between performer and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application check: Is there a violation present?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific expectation being violated and its domain (moral, social, linguistic, physical, etc.). Without a clear violation, the material is unlikely to elicit humor under this theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application check: Is the violation simultaneously benign?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the violation simultaneously benign (alternative norm available, weak commitment, distance)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mechanisms such as norm detachment, psychological distance, or reinterpretation are present to make the violation feel harmless to the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application check: Are both perceptions held at once?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are both perceptions (violation and benignness) held at once by the audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the audience can cognitively/affectively maintain both stances simultaneously; if not, the joke will likely misfire (too threatening or too banal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application check: Does the audience have appropriate distance from the violation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience have appropriate distance from the violation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social, temporal, spatial, and fictive distance for your target audience. Lack of distance can make a violation feel real and threatening rather than benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: When humor fails (failure modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can fail either because the situation depicts a violation that does not seem benign (too aggressive/threatening) or because it depicts a benign situation that has no violation (too safe/boring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these failure modes as diagnostic checks: if the material reads as merely offensive/dangerous, reduce perceived threat or increase benign cues; if it is merely innocuous, introduce a clear violation or unexpected incongruity.
